Your course books don’t cover this, so this is from my general knowledge:

HTTPS secures a web connection by layering TLS (Transport Layer Security) over HTTP. When a browser contacts a site, the TLS handshake begins. First, the server sends its digital certificate containing a public key, which the browser verifies (e.g., signed by a trusted CA). The browser then generates a random “pre‑master secret,” encrypts it with the server’s public key, and sends it back. Only the server can decrypt this value with its private key. Both sides then derive the same symmetric session keys from the pre‑master secret. These symmetric keys are used for the actual data transfer because they are fast, providing confidentiality (encryption) and integrity (MAC/HMAC). Thus, the heavy asymmetric cryptography is used just once to exchange a secret, after which all HTTP payloads are encrypted with the shared symmetric key, protecting the communication from eavesdropping and tampering.
